title: Write your own operators
summary: Extension methods with yield return that chain like the built-in ones, stay lazy, and validate their arguments at the right time.

steps.title: An operator is an extension method
body: `Where` is not magic. It is an **extension method** on `IEnumerable<T>` written with `yield return`. You can write your own, and they chain like the built-in ones.
public static IEnumerable<T> WhereNot<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> test)
- the first parameter has `this` in front: that is what lets you call it with a dot
- generic in `T`, so it works for any item type

steps.prompt: Complete the operator so `words.LongerThan(3)` works and stays lazy.
code: public static IEnumerable<string> LongerThan(__1__ IEnumerable<string> source, int n)
steps.explain: `this` on the first parameter makes it an extension method. `yield return` hands out one item at a time; a plain `return` would not compile here, because the method returns a sequence.

steps.title: WhereNot and TakeEvery
prompt: Write a `static class MyLinq` with two lazy extension methods, using `yield return`:
- `WhereNot<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> test)`: the items for which `test` is **false**.
- `TakeEvery<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int n)`: every `n`th item, starting with the first. `[a, b, c, d, e].TakeEvery(2)` is `[a, c, e]`.
Both must work on an **infinite** sequence: the tests use them on `1, 2, 3, ...` forever, followed by `Take`.

public static IEnumerable<T> TakeEvery<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int n)
solution: public static IEnumerable<T> WhereNot<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> test)
public static IEnumerable<T> TakeEvery<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int n)
template: Dojo.Eq("WhereNot(even) on 1..6", new List<int> { 1, 3, 5 }, Enumerable.Range(1, 6).WhereNot(n => n % 2 == 0).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("WhereNot on strings", new List<string> { "INFO up", "WARN cpu" }, new[] { "DEBUG a", "INFO up", "DEBUG b", "WARN cpu" }.WhereNot(l => l.StartsWith("DEBUG")).ToList());
var dojoForever = Enumerable.Range(1, int.MaxValue).Select(n => { dojoPulled++; return n; });
Dojo.Eq("TakeEvery(2) on an endless source, then Take(3)", new List<int> { 1, 3, 5 }, dojoForever.TakeEvery(2).Take(3).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("only 5 items were pulled from the source", 5, dojoPulled);
Dojo.Eq("WhereNot on an endless source", new List<int> { 1, 2, 4 }, dojoForever.WhereNot(n => n % 3 == 0).Take(3).ToList());

forbid.message: Does not call ToList, ToArray or Where

hints: `WhereNot` is a `foreach` with an `if (!test(item)) yield return item;`.
For `TakeEvery`, keep a counter `i` and yield when `i % n == 0`.
Do not collect into a list first: that would never finish on an endless source.

steps.title: When does the body run?
body: Calling an iterator method runs **none** of its body. The body starts at the first `MoveNext`, and pauses at each `yield return`. That is what makes it lazy, and it has one unwanted side effect: **argument checks are lazy too**.
public static IEnumerable<T[]> Batch<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int size)
var batches = orders.Batch(0);   // no error here
foreach (var b in batches)       // throws here
The built-in operators throw **at the call**. To do the same, split the method: a plain method that checks and then returns a local iterator.

steps.title: Operators that remember
body: An iterator can keep **state** between items, in ordinary local variables. That makes operators that look at neighbours easy to write.
**Pairwise**: each item with the one before it. Useful for "change since last reading":
**Window(size)**: a sliding window, for moving averages:
For `Window`, a `Queue<T>` holds the last `size` items: `Enqueue` the new one, `Dequeue` the oldest once it is too long, and `yield return queue.ToArray()` when it is full.

steps.prompt: Arrange the body of `Pairwise`, which yields each item paired with the one before it.
lines: public static IEnumerable<(T, T)> Pairwise<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source)
steps.explain: Take the first item by hand (stopping at once if there is none), then for each next item yield the pair **before** moving `prev` along. Swap those two lines and every pair would be an item paired with itself.

steps.title: Pairwise and Window
prompt: Write a `static class Neighbours` with two lazy extension methods:
- `Pairwise<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source)` returning `IEnumerable<(T, T)>`: each item paired with the one before. Fewer than two items gives nothing.
- `Window<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int size)` returning `IEnumerable<T[]>`: every run of `size` neighbours, in order. `[1, 2, 3, 4].Window(3)` is `[1, 2, 3]`, `[2, 3, 4]`.
Both must work on an endless source.
starter: public static IEnumerable<(T, T)> Pairwise<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source)
public static IEnumerable<T[]> Window<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int size)
solution: public static IEnumerable<(T, T)> Pairwise<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source)
public static IEnumerable<T[]> Window<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int size)
template: Dojo.Eq("changes between readings", new List<int> { 3, -4, 6 }, new[] { 10, 13, 9, 15 }.Pairwise().Select(p => p.Item2 - p.Item1).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("Pairwise of one item is empty", 0, new[] { 1 }.Pairwise().Count());
Dojo.Eq("Pairwise of nothing is empty", 0, new int[0].Pairwise().Count());
Dojo.Eq("Pairwise on an endless source", (2, 3), Enumerable.Range(1, int.MaxValue).Pairwise().ElementAt(1));
Dojo.Eq("Window(3) of 1..4", new List<string> { "1,2,3", "2,3,4" }, new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }.Window(3).Select(w => string.Join(",", w)).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("moving average", new List<double> { 2, 3, 4 }, new[] { 1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0 }.Window(3).Select(w => w.Average()).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("Window larger than the source", 0, new[] { 1, 2 }.Window(3).Count());
Dojo.Eq("Window on an endless source", "3,4", string.Join(",", Enumerable.Range(1, int.MaxValue).Window(2).ElementAt(2)));
hints: `Pairwise`: remember the previous item in a variable, and a `bool` for "is this the first one?".
`Window`: a `Queue<T>`. Enqueue each item, dequeue when the count goes over `size`.
Yield `window.ToArray()` (a copy) whenever `window.Count == size`. Yielding the queue itself would hand out one object that keeps changing.

steps.title: Sidekick: your own Batch
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk list --all` prints your tasks ten at a time and `sk import-csv` saves in batches of 50. Both use an operator you write now.

Write a `static class SidekickLinq` with `public static IEnumerable<T[]> Batch<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int size)`: consecutive groups of `size` items as arrays, the last one possibly shorter. `[1..7].Batch(3)` is `[1,2,3]`, `[4,5,6]`, `[7]`. Do not use `Chunk`.

It must be lazy (it works on an endless source), **and** it must check its arguments **at the call**, before anything enumerates it: `ArgumentNullException` for a null source, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` when `size < 1`. Use the split from the "When does the body run?" card.
The tests also batch a few of your `TaskItem`s and print them with your `Ids.Format`.

solution: public static IEnumerable<T[]> Batch<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, int size)
if (size < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(size), "A batch holds at least one item.");
static IEnumerable<T[]> Iterate(IEnumerable<T> source, int size)
template: Dojo.Eq("Batch(3) of 1..7", new List<string> { "1,2,3", "4,5,6", "7" }, Enumerable.Range(1, 7).Batch(3).Select(b => string.Join(",", b)).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("an exact fit has no short batch", 2, Enumerable.Range(1, 4).Batch(2).Count());
Dojo.Eq("nothing gives no batches", 0, new int[0].Batch(5).Count());
Dojo.Eq("works on an endless source", new[] { 5, 6 }, Enumerable.Range(1, int.MaxValue).Batch(2).ElementAt(2));
Dojo.Eq("a kept batch is not overwritten by the next", new[] { 1, 2 }, Enumerable.Range(1, 4).Batch(2).ToList()[0]);
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("Batch(0) throws at the call, not later", () => { var dojoLater = new[] { 1 }.Batch(0); });
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentNullException>("a null source throws at the call", () => { var dojoLater = ((IEnumerable<int>)null!).Batch(2); });

hints: Move all the `yield` code into a local function `static IEnumerable<T[]> Iterate(IEnumerable<T> source, int size)` inside `Batch`.
`Batch` itself has no `yield`: `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source);`, check `size`, then `return Iterate(source, size);`.
Inside `Iterate`, fill a `List<T>`; when it reaches `size`, `yield return buffer.ToArray();` and `Clear()` it. After the loop, yield what is left if it is not empty.
steps.explain: Splitting the checks from the iterator is what the real `Chunk` does: misuse fails where it is written, while the work stays lazy. Returning a fresh array per batch means a caller can keep a batch after asking for the next one.
